Evidence: the Git 2.46 HTML manual installed on this machine (C:/Program Files/Git/mingw64/share/doc/git-doc/, 'Last updated 2024-07-29'), which is the pinned version's own documentation, rather than git-scm.com; and the blobs at tag stage-0 read straight out of examples/don-hang/.git object store (the `git` CLI and tools/extract-code were refused by the sandbox, so the tag object 664d38a0… was dereferenced by hand to commit ff911b0b…, and every file below comes from that commit's tree, not from the working copy).

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-bisect(1), 'Basic bisect commands: start, bad, good', verbatim: "$ git bisect start" / "$ git bisect bad                 # Current version is bad" / "$ git bisect good v2.6.13-rc2    # v2.6.13-rc2 is known to be good". The comment on the second line is the documented no-argument behaviour the lesson states; the SYNOPSIS makes the revision optional: "git bisect (bad|new|<term-new>) [<rev>]", "git bisect (good|old|<term-old>) [<rev>...]".
claim_verdicts.source: Installed Git 2.46 manual, git-bisect.html lines 468-511 (SYNOPSIS; Basic bisect commands)

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-bisect(1): "Once you have specified at least one bad and one good commit, git bisect selects a commit in the middle of that range of history, checks it out, and outputs something similar to the following: Bisecting: 675 revisions left to test after this (roughly 10 steps)"; after one answer "Bisecting: 337 revisions left to test after this (roughly 9 steps)" — the range halves per answer; "Eventually there will be no more revisions left to inspect, and the command will print out a description of the first bad commit."

DESCRIPTION: "You use it by first telling it a 'bad' commit that is known to contain the bug, and a 'good' commit that is known to be before the bug was introduced… It continues narrowing down the range until it finds the exact commit that introduced the change." So bad bounds the answer at-or-before, good after. Nothing on the page re-checks an answer; the only escape offered is "$ git bisect skip   # Current version cannot be tested". Monotonicity is never stated as something Git verifies — it is the reader's assumption, as the lesson says.

Doc gives the event, not the format: "the command will print out a description of the first bad commit". Execution gives the format — the capture committed at stage-0: "b3472f64d738ebe52e4441e8d15ca273d88d439a is the first bad commit" / "commit b3472f64…" / Author / Date / "    Round the total down to millions" / " total.sh | 2 +-" / " 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)" — full id, message and the files changed, exactly as the lesson says.

git-bisect(1), 'Bisect reset': "After a bisect session, to clean up the bisection state and return to the original HEAD, issue the following command: $ git bisect reset" and "By default, this will return your tree to the commit that was checked out before git bisect start." Execution agrees: the capture ends "Previous HEAD position was 09c8526 Add a second product" / "Switched to branch 'main'" — back on the branch the session started from.

Git's own estimate is log2 of what is left: "675 revisions left to test after this (roughly 10 steps)" — ceil(log2 675)=10; "337 … (roughly 9 steps)" — ceil(log2 337)=9. log2(1000)=9.97, so "a thousand in about ten" holds. The four-commit figure is execution, not arithmetic alone: between the marks and the result the capture shows exactly two runs of the check (lines 9-14), and ceil(log2 4)=2.

The verdict is supplied by the tester and taken as final: "You should now compile the checked-out version and test it. If that version works correctly, type $ git bisect good" / "If that version is broken, type $ git bisect bad". The manual offers no way to revise or re-check an answer; the only special case is a commit that cannot be tested ("git bisect skip", exit code 125 in a run script). So a flipped answer is believed and the half holding the cause is dropped. Not reproduced here: the playground lives inside the lab container.

gitrevisions(7): "A suffix ~<n> to a revision parameter means the commit object that is the <n>th generation ancestor of the named commit object, following only the first parents". git-switch(1): "-d, --detach: Switch to a commit for inspection and discardable experiments" and, under EXAMPLES, "To switch back to the previous branch before we switched to mytopic…: $ git switch -". The playground's main is linear, so "four steps back" and the first-parent rule coincide.
claim_verdicts.source: Installed Git 2.46 manual, gitrevisions.html line 694ff; git-switch.html lines 552-557, 733-738

claim_verdicts.evidence: git-playground/build-history.sh at stage-0 commits 6 times on main (price list; total.sh+test.sh; second product; Round the total down to millions; Explain the rounding; README). HEAD~4 is 'Add total.sh and a check for it', where prices.txt holds one item, so awk's sum equals total.sh's output → "ok", and test.sh's last statement is that echo under `set -eu`, i.e. exit 0; bisect-demo.sh line 16 runs it bare under `set -euo pipefail` and the capture continues to line 26. claim_verdicts.evidence: Capture at the tag, verbatim: "b3472f64d738ebe52e4441e8d15ca273d88d439a is the first bad commit", "    Round the total down to millions", " total.sh | 2 +-", " 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)" — the lesson's output block reproduces these four lines exactly. The added condition holds: build-history.sh line 64 makes that commit with one sed rewriting the single line `echo "$total"`, so the 1+/1- is that one line replaced, not two separate edits.

build-history.sh, commit 'Round the total down to millions': sed -i 's|^echo "$total"$|echo $(( (total / 1000000) * 1000000 ))|' total.sh. test.sh computes `expected` with awk '{ sum += $2 } END { print sum }' prices.txt, which the rounding never touches. At HEAD prices.txt is 1250000 + 450000 = 1700000 and (1700000/1000000)*1000000 = 1000000 in shell integer arithmetic — exactly the captured "expected 1700000, got 1000000".

build-history.sh exports GIT_AUTHOR_NAME/EMAIL and GIT_COMMITTER_NAME/EMAIL before any commit and save() exports GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE from its argument; its comment states the intent: "Fixed author, committer and dates, so that every commit id below is the same on every machine and the lessons can quote them." The remaining inputs are fixed too, since line 5 re-executes the script inside the lab container ([ -f /.dockerenv ] || exec …/lab-run.sh), so git version and file modes do not vary. The quoted id b3472f64… is the one the committed capture shows.

Opinion, but both halves are documented. Input: the manual asks only for a bad commit, a good commit and your test — no suspicion is an input ("You use it by first telling it a 'bad' commit… and a 'good' commit"). Cost: "Bisecting: 675 revisions left to test after this (roughly 10 steps)" shows the step count as log2 of the range, so about ten runs stand against 675 diffs to read.

"finished no slower" is what the arithmetic supports: squashing 'Round the total down to millions' and 'Explain the rounding' leaves three candidates and ceil(log2 3)=2 — the same two runs the capture shows; squashing all four leaves one candidate and no runs at all. The second half ("names a change too large to read") is about the named commit's own diff, which here is one file and one line.

The safety half is documented: git bisect "selects a commit in the middle of that range of history", so only the range between the ends is ever tested and nothing re-checks an end. The cost half is stated too strongly. By the lesson's own model — Git's estimate is log2 of the range: 675 → "roughly 10 steps", 337 → "roughly 9 steps" — each doubling of the range adds one step, so "a step or two" buys an end at most about four times further back, not an arbitrarily distant one.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: prefer one older than you suspect: each doubling of the range adds only one more step, so an end a few times further back costs a step or two, while an end that in fact already fails puts the breaking commit outside the search

claim_verdicts.evidence: Git's estimate is log2 of the revisions left — "675 revisions left to test after this (roughly 10 steps)", ceil(log2 675)=10; "337 … (roughly 9 steps)", ceil(log2 337)=9. The claim's arithmetic checks out: ceil(log2 24)=5 and ceil(log2 64)=6, so any range in that band costs five or six runs, which is what §6 says and what quiz q6 asks (ceil(log2 60)=6).

The blob at tag stage-0 is 26 lines; the excerpt is lines=10-23. What remains is line 24 `git bisect run ./test.sh`, an empty line 25 and line 26 `git bisect reset >/dev/null` — two commands. Nothing below "so ask Git to find the first bad one:" has another source.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Capture lines 9-14, verbatim: "running './test.sh'" / "expected 1700000, got 1000000" / "Bisecting: 0 revisions left to test after this (roughly 0 steps)" / "[09c85269f0ee4cc7b6a0f856acca27d5aa3267bd] Add a second product" / "running './test.sh'" / "ok" — two runs of the check with one checkout between them: the failure at the midpoint Git was already standing on after line 23, then ok at 09c85269 'Add a second product'. §7's "it fails once … and prints ok once" follows from the same six lines.

The manual shipped with the pinned client ends git-switch's DESCRIPTION with "THIS COMMAND IS EXPERIMENTAL. THE BEHAVIOR MAY CHANGE." git-checkout at the same version carries both moves: SYNOPSIS "git checkout [-q] [-f] [-m] [--detach] <commit>" with the "--detach" option, and "you can also specify - which is synonymous to @{-1}".

issues.quote: the check failed at the commit Git had already stopped on, and printed `ok` at the next one
issues.text: "the next one" means the next commit Git stopped on, but reads as the next commit in history. The capture shows the second run at 09c85269 'Add a second product', which is older than the commit that failed — and §4 has just taught that a good answer means the first bad commit is later, so a learner reading "next" chronologically gets a passing commit after a failing one, i.e. the monotonicity they were told to assume, broken. The rest of the sentence matches capture lines 9-14 exactly.
issues.fix: Name the order: "… the check failed at the commit Git had already stopped on, and printed `ok` at the next commit Git stopped on, an older one." The same wording fits §7 step 3, which already names both printed lines.

issues.quote: prefer one older than you suspect, since a distant end only costs a step or two
issues.text: The cost is stated without its bound. By the log₂ rule the lesson teaches one section later, each doubling of the range adds one step, so "a step or two" covers an end about two to four times further back; an end a hundred times further back costs about seven more runs. As written a reader can take "distant" to mean the repository's first commit at no cost, which §4's own arithmetic contradicts.
issues.fix: Give the rule instead of the estimate: "prefer one older than you suspect: each doubling of the range adds only one more step, so an end a few times further back costs a step or two, while an end that in fact already fails puts the breaking commit outside the search."

issues.text: I re-read this twice. "The listing" can be the code block or the output block, and the two commands are never written down, so I cannot line them up against the by-hand steps in the next sentence. What they do is stated, and the sentence after tells me exactly what the `...` hides, so I was not stuck — but I scrolled back three times to check I had not missed a line of the excerpt.
issues.fix: Say which listing: replace "The listing stops two commands before the end of the script" with "The excerpt above stops two commands before the end of the script".

issues.text: "the next one" reads as the next commit in history, and that would mean a commit passing after one that failed — the opposite of the assumption section 4 told me the search rests on. I stopped, then guessed it means the next commit Git stopped on, which must be an older one.
issues.fix: Write "and printed `ok` at the next commit Git stopped on, an older one".
issues.quote: the check failed at the commit Git had already stopped on, and printed `ok` at the next one

issues.text: The output block shows `b3472f64d738ebe52e4441e8d15ca273d88d439a`, the prose shows `b3472f6`, and Expected result shows `b3472f6…`. Nothing says that a short prefix names the same commit, so I compared the two strings character by character before deciding they were the same one.
issues.fix: Add the bridge inside the sentence: "Git names `b3472f6` — the first characters of the long id in the listing — and prints it".

issues.text: I counted on my fingers and got three. Between the commit four back and the commit I am standing on there are three commits; the fourth is the one I am standing on, which is an end, not "in between". I read the sentence twice before deciding the count includes the newest commit.
issues.fix: Replace "one of the four commits in between" with "one of the four commits made since then".
issues.quote: So one of the four commits in between turned the first answer into the second, and two of them touch `total.sh`.

issues.text: This arrives with no instruction attached. I do not know what "experimental" costs me, and the sentence says `git checkout` does the same without telling me which one to type. At the one moment the lesson asks me to work by hand, I still do not know which command that is.
issues.fix: Close the sentence with the decision: "…and `git checkout` makes the same two moves, so either command works here."
issues.quote: Git 2.46's own manual labels `git switch` experimental, and `git checkout` makes the same two moves.

issues.text: Here `log₂` is used as if it were a thing you can have the same of. Section 4 gave me "the number of steps is the number of halvings — about log₂ of the commits between the ends", which I followed; "the same log₂ either way" made me stop and translate it back into that sentence.
issues.fix: Replace "because the work is the same log₂ either way" with "because the number of halvings is the same either way".
issues.quote: The less you know, the more it saves, because the work is the same log₂ either way.
